expl.label: Words inside inline section headings/subtitles embedded in running web text
expl.positive_pole: Content words of a short title-case heading or subheading that appears on its own line after a paragraph of body text, e.g. 'Innovation Still Has a Ways to Go', 'Better Safe Than Sorry', 'Invest in the Best', 'Price War in Imported Assault Weapons', 'Trick Your Brain Into…', 'ROGERS MAKING STRIDES'. It fires on tokens after the first word of the heading, peaks on the second to fourth word (the key noun or verb, such as Still/has, Revolution, Reliability, World, Best, Foundation, Value, Here, Out), and often carries onto the newline that ends the heading. It is strongest for catchy, idiomatic or slogan-like headings in blog, article or marketing prose.
expl.negative_pole: Weak, at most about -2. Appears on structural or listing text that is not a catchy heading: table-of-contents entries, numbered list items ('1 Synopsis', 'About the Author'), report-style titles, stats lines, product spec strings and the newline after them. There is also a scattered -1 on ordinary body-text tokens.
expl.rubric: Background is 0 for nearly all tokens, including normal prose, list items and metadata. When a newline is followed by a short title-like phrase and body text resumes after it, score that heading as follows. The first word gets about 0 to +1. Following function words ('the', 'in', 'of', 'to', 'and') get +1 to +5. The main content word gets +5 to +10, with +7 to +10 for idiomatic or slogan headings. The newline right after the heading gets +2 to +9. Plain descriptive headings ('Book Format', 'When To Go', 'Digital World') get +2 to +4. Technical or definitional headings (chemical names) get about +3. The first word of the heading and the following body text drop back to about 0. Score -1 to -2 for table-of-contents or numbered outline entries, report-like section names ('Synopsis', 'About the Author'), stats or spec lines, and the newline after a list item. Long full-sentence titles in document lists get small negatives.

expl.label: Span-opening tokens (quotes, $, pre-number space): reported speech/money (+) vs labels/commands/dates (−)
expl.positive_pole: The opening token of a quoted span or quantity whose content is a quotation, title or name. Typical cases are an opening quote mark that begins reported speech or a quoted statement after 'he said,', 'told X.', 'explained:' or 'said:' (e.g. ''If you want…'' he said, '' / "If I was…" / “We'll make mistakes”). Also opening quotes or apostrophes before organization names and titles (“We the People”, ‘Made in Japan’, ‘Abdullah’, “The Roof Clinic…”, "For his outstanding research"). Also '$' before a monetary amount ($7,500, $200, $13 billion) and the space before '21st century'. The quote or '$' token itself carries the peak (+4 to +6). The first word inside the quote often gets a smaller +1 to +4.
expl.negative_pole: The same kinds of opening tokens when the span is a short UI label, an imperative command, a slogan, or a single word or term being mentioned. Examples are button names (click the “Get it” / “Sign in” / "Open File" button), voice commands (“Find Nearest…”), shirt slogans ("Wife to One") and words being defined (and 'masturbate'). Also an opening quote before a yelled imperative (yells, "Hey kid, get…") and a colon in transcript dialogue right before a short reply (Me: Yes…). Also the space or digit opening a day-of-month in a date (born on 22nd May; October 25th). These reach −5 to −10, carried by the quote mark, colon or space token.
expl.rubric: Background: most tokens are 0, with frequent scattered ±1 noise on ordinary content words (often −1) and on digits in numbers, codes and phone numbers (+1 to +3). For an opening quote mark or apostrophe, '$', or a space/colon right before a quoted or numeric span, decide what follows. If it introduces a sentence of reported speech, a name or a title, assign +3 to +6. Assign +5 for '$' before a money figure. If it introduces a button or menu label, a command, a slogan, a mentioned word or a day-of-month date, assign −5 to −10. Assign −8 to −10 for button labels, slogans and birth-date days. Ambiguous or short quoted phrases with mixed character get about ±2 to ±3. Closing quotes are about +1 and are not peaks. Tokens inside the span: the first word gets about +1 to +4 on the positive side and is near 0 otherwise. Plain numbers without '$', and prose with no quoted span, stay within ±1.

expl.label: Closing/completing a structure: 'click OK to close the dialog box', endif, unquote
expl.positive_pole: Tokens that close off or finish a structure or sequence. The strongest case, by far, is software UI instructions about dismissing a dialog: in 'Click OK to close the dialog box', 'OK' scores about +9, 'close' about +6 and 'box' about +10, and 'click OK' alone scores about +7. Related closers fire more weakly: '.endif' (+5), 'unquote' after a quote (+4), the closing corner '+' or '|' of an ASCII table border (+6 to +10), and SQL tail clauses like 'GROUP BY' / 'ON' (+2 to +3). It also fires on complementary completions: the remainder number in '41 percent male and 59 percent female' (the '9' is about +5), 'the other' at the end of 'each one ... the other' (+3), and endings such as 'passed away' (+2 to +3) or the final 'not' in 'do not distribute' (+3).
expl.negative_pole: Weak, max about -4. It fires on recipe and procedure steps that follow cooking, where food is left to rest. Examples: the imperative 'Cool' after 'Bake ... until golden' (-2 to -4), 'Keep warm', 'and set aside', 'and let sit', 'and place'. There are scattered -1 to -2 values on other sequential-instruction verbs and connectives, such as 'then' or 'booting', and occasionally on narrative details like 'hanged himself'.
expl.rubric: Background is 0 for nearly all tokens; about 99.9% of tokens are below 1. Assign +7 to +10 only to UI dialog-dismissal phrases: 'OK' and 'box' in 'click OK to close the dialog box', and 'close' at about +6. Assign +4 to +6 to explicit structure closers: 'endif', 'unquote', the final corner of an ASCII table border, and a complementary percentage completing a 100% split. Assign +1 to +3 to softer endings and completions: 'the other', 'passed away', the 'not' in 'do not distribute', SQL 'GROUP BY'/'ON', and closing list numbers. Ordinary prose, plain numbers and opening tokens get 0; scattered ±1 noise is common. Negative values: -2 to -4 on a recipe 'Cool' / 'Keep warm' / 'set aside' step after cooking; -1 on surrounding instruction connectives.

expl.label: Diffuse, sparse neuron: spikes on predictable mid-phrase tokens and paragraph breaks
expl.positive_pole:
Rare large spikes, with no single clean theme. The biggest (+10) fell on a sentence-final '.
' that closes an explanatory paragraph and comes right before a new section heading ('...flea problem that is already there.
' followed by 'Limit Outdoor Exposure'). Other strong spikes (+4 to +8) land on a word inside a fixed multiword unit whose continuation is highly predictable. Examples: 'number' in 'features a number of', 'example' in 'significant example of', 'of' in 'warmth of the', 'site' in 'third party site', 'Advantage' in 'Medicare Advantage Plan', 'tag' in 'franchise tag', 'Out' in 'Tapped Out', 'ewire' in 'Primewire', 'firmly' in 'anchored firmly to', 'could'/'might' in hedged 'which could affect' / 'this might lead'. Weak +1 to +3 values are common on ordinary connectives in flowing prose: 'and', 'of', 'to', 'can', 'will', commas, '.', '
'. They are slightly more frequent in promotional, advice or bio-style text.
expl.negative_pole: Weak, max about -4. Mostly falls on tokens in the middle of a prepositional or verbal phrase. Examples: 'to' in 'From user-generated resources to', 'arising' in 'trauma arising from', 'typically' in 'is typically served', 'may' in 'who may be searching', 'by' in 'out of 5 by', 'upon' in 'Stratford upon Avon', 'getting a', 'U.S.', 'aggregation'. Diffuse -1 values also appear on proper nouns, team/airline names, dates, numbers, and list items with commas. The '.\n' that ends a descriptive paragraph can occasionally go -4 instead of positive.
expl.rubric: Background: about 90% of tokens are 0. About 10% sit at ±1, scattered roughly evenly: +1 on connectives and auxiliaries in running prose, -1 on names, numbers, dates and list items. Assign +2 to +3 to 'of'/'in'/'and' inside common collocations and to hedging modals ('could', 'might', 'will'). Assign +4 to +6 to the head word of a fixed multiword unit right before its predictable continuation ('a number [of]', 'example [of]', 'Medicare Advantage [Plan]', 'third party site'). Reserve +8 to +10 for the rare cases: a paragraph-ending '.\n' just before a section heading in how-to/advice articles, and very strong 'a number of' constructions. Negative values: -2 to -4 on mid-phrase prepositions and adverbs ('to', 'by', 'upon', 'typically', 'arising') and on some descriptive paragraph-final newlines. Never exceed about -4. Most similar-looking tokens stay near 0, so predict sparingly.

expl.label: Target/container/tool noun: what something is converted into, placed in, or handled with
expl.positive_pole: Fires on the head noun naming the destination, container, format or tool of an operation. This is usually a technical type or product name in software and docs: `Money` objects, an xml doc, arrays, ndarray, solids, an electrical signal, smart layers, Lightroom, UXPin, Joda Time, Oracle Support, item record, Issue Date. Kitchen and craft containers also count (a bowl, a colander), as do completions of operation phrases (open the wim up, cut them out, Base 5, composed of, IPv4 address manipulation). The strongest case is the noun closing a conversion phrase like 'converting X into `Money` objects'. Here the type name gets about +8, its backtick about +2, and the final noun 'objects' gets +10. Activation sits on the last token of the product or type name, or on the head noun, not on the verb ('converting', 'convert').
expl.negative_pole: Weak only, mostly -1 to -2.5. Two main sources: (1) runs of digits in long numbers, such as timestamp fractions (.00000), URL ID strings and measurements like 16' 5"; (2) step-by-step physical instructions in recipes and crafts. In (2) the hits fall on prepositions and placement words ('place ... on parchment paper', 'under running cold water', 'to refrigerate', 'hands on his shoulders to brace'), with -1 to -2 on 'on', 'to', 'under', 'for'. Navigation text such as 'Search by' also gets about -2.
expl.rubric: Background is about 0; most tokens fall within ±0.5. Narrative and promotional prose often carries a diffuse +1 on scattered function and content words; this is not meaningful. Score +8 to +10 for a type or object noun that is the explicit result of a conversion or creation phrase in code or library descriptions ('into `Money` objects'). Score +3 to +5 for a software product or tool name, or a technical data structure, named as the thing used or targeted (Oracle Support, UXPin, xml doc, arrays, Base 5, 'up' in 'open the wim up', Issue Date, 'can' in 'so i can access'). Score +2 to +3 for a container noun in a recipe ('in a bowl', 'colander') or a destination noun after 'convert it to an' ('electrical signal', solids, smart layers, Lightroom, Joda Time, item record). Score +1 for nearby determiners and prepositions in such phrases ('to', 'an', 'as'). Score -1 to -2.5 for digit runs and for placement prepositions in physical procedure text. Verbs of conversion, generic nouns without a tool or target role, and plain numbers score about 0 or slightly negative.

expl.label: Positive inside predictable boilerplate; negative where metadata gives way to new content
expl.positive_pole:
Tokens inside formulaic, memorized, or template-like text, where the next tokens are strongly predictable from familiar web or code boilerplate. The activation lands on the token just before the predictable continuation. Examples:
- 'Q&A «for» professional and enthusiast programmers' (StackExchange tagline)
- 'Funding«:» This work was supported'
- 'itunes«.apple».com/us/«album»/'
- 'Mysql::Error«:» Cannot delete'
- 'JOIN («SELECT»'
- '->«columns»('id')'
- 'enter the following «command»:'
- 'names have the «form» <simpleId>'
- 'Future compatibility is not «guaranteed»'
- 'Investors, take «note»!'
- 'everyone here «at» [Company]'
- 'As you'll see in «this» video'
- 'Read more«↵»0 Comments'
- ASCII tree '| «||»' and citation '(2005«),»'
These are code keywords, URL paths, legal/academic boilerplate, and stock phrases.
expl.negative_pole:
Two kinds of tokens drive the negative pole.
1. The delimiter or boundary token where a metadata, header, or boilerplate block ends and free-form novel content begins:
- 'Abstract «:»' (-10)
- 'Abstract:«||»'
- news datelines 'NEW YORK (AP«)» «-»' and '(AP) «—»'
- the newline after 'Statistics from Altmetric.com'
- 'Transcript«↵»'
- 'Clicking «here»' / 'CLICK «HERE»'
- 'BEGIN PGP SIGNED «MESSAGE»'
- 'geography":↵«...»'
- the journal series letter in 'Technology «A» 4,'
2. The Unicode hyphen '‐' (U+2010) inside compound words: 're‐parametrizations' -6, 'non‐identified' -9, 'high‐alkali' -5.
expl.rubric:
Background: about 8% of tokens sit at ±1 with scattered weak ±1 noise, mostly +1 on function words in flowing prose and -1 on content nouns and adjectives; magnitudes of 3 or more are very rare.

Positive values:
- +3 to +5 (rarely higher): the pivot token of a well-known template, code idiom, or URL path. Examples are 'Q&A for' +5, 'JOIN (SELECT' +5, '.apple' +3/+4, 'album' +5, 'columns' +4, 'Funding:' +4, 'command' +4.
- +2: tokens in tree art, citations, or sales phrases.

Negative values:
- -5 to -10: the colon or delimiter right after 'Abstract' in report metadata, the closing ')' or dash of AP datelines, and U+2010 hyphens.
- -3 to -5: 'here' in click-here link prompts, the newline after a metadata or attribution line, and '...' before an excerpt.

What stays near 0: ordinary hyphens and ordinary prose, unless the text is formulaic.

expl.label: Negative: tokens inside technical terms being defined or explained; weak diffuse positive
expl.positive_pole: Weak and diffuse, rarely above +2. It appears on function and content words in procedural, financial or obligational prose. Examples: 'the amount you have to pay', 'total minimum contribution', 'pay 20% of the total as a', 'Deposit of 30% minimum required on', 'self-assessment', 'convince him to'. It also shows up in polite requests ('if you could just take a moment of your time to') and in sports recaps ('even his record at 9 and 9', 'answered in the bottom half'). It often spans several consecutive tokens at about +1. Digits and '%' in money or percentage figures get about +1.
expl.negative_pole: Fires on tokens of a technical or domain term, usually a compound noun, that the passage is introducing, defining or explaining. The strongest values fall on the core subword of the term's head, especially when it is being defined. Examples: 'What is absorption costing? / Absorption costing goes by…' gives -7 on 'absorption' and -10 on 'orption', with -1 to -4 on 'costing'. Others: 'Hal|ogen' bulbs (-3), hip 'dys|pl|asia' (-2 to -3 on 'pl'), 'pass through entities' (-3/-2), 'S Corporations' (-2), 'Diastolic pressure' (-2), 'fixed rate' (-2), 'amino acids' (-2), 'array index' (-2). Weaker cases include an ellipsis mid-explanation ('you can…use them', -3), a label colon ('UPC Code:', -3) and 'Reviewed by' (-2). Magnitude grows when the term is being defined (questions like 'What is X?' or 'X is…'), when it is repeated, and when it is rare or jargon-like.
expl.rubric:
Background is 0 for almost all tokens; only about 0.02% of tokens reach |value| ≥ 1. Ordinary prose, names and common words get 0. Assign negatives only to tokens of specialized terms in explanatory or educational text:
- Repeated, defined jargon heads ('Absorption' in 'Absorption costing goes by many names'): -7 to -10.
- Typical jargon tokens in explanations, usually the middle subword or the first word of a compound: -2 to -4.
- Modifier or second words of the term: -1 to -2.
- Tokens in casual mentions of a technical term: -1.

Positives are small:
- +1 (occasionally +2) on tokens in payment, percentage or obligation phrases.
- +1 on 'to' or 'into' after verbs like convince, baited or need you.
- +1 on 'more' in 'read more' and '...More...'.
- +1 on sports-recap phrasing.

Do not give large positives; positive values almost never exceed +2. Not every technical word fires: plain everyday nouns and non-explanatory product listings stay near 0.

expl.label: Small group of people as a joint unit (+) vs. distributive or enumerated counts (−)
expl.positive_pole: Tokens that refer to a small set of people or animate entities treated as one collective unit, especially pairs and trios acting or described together. Typical triggers are 'Two Friends', 'tandem of', 'trio', 'twins', 'brothers', 'sisters', 'young men from different', 'both … and', 'they' (when referring back to a pair or group), 'on either side', 'two vehicles' (in a collision between two). Activation lands on the group noun or quantifier ('friends', 'trio', 'twins', 'tandem', 'of' after 'tandem' or 'group') or on the anaphoric 'they'/'both'. It is strongest in narrative or descriptive prose about people jointly doing or being something.
expl.negative_pole: Distributive or multiplicative counting, where a number applies to each member or to items in an itemized list rather than to one joint group. Examples: 'each for two nights)' (−10 on the ')'), 'three couples' (−7), 'by each party,' (−5/−6), 'three, two-bedroom flats' (−6 on 'two'), '3 lunches and 3 dinners' (−5 on the second '3'), 'on both Saturday…' (−5), 'two sets of' (−5 on 'of'), 'every two miles' (−4), 'fourth and eighth grade' (−3/−4), '20 characters', '(3″)', list colons and line breaks in spec or inventory lists. Activation lands on the number, 'each', 'every', 'of', closing punctuation, or a newline right after a per-unit quantity.
expl.rubric:
Background is 0 for nearly all tokens; only about 0.1% of tokens reach |value| ≥ 1.

Positive values:
- +4 to +5: a group-of-people noun in a clear joint context ('Two Friends Risked', 'trio of', 'tandem of', 'both' linking two named entities).
- +2 to +3: 'twins', 'brothers', 'sisters', 'two' meaning a pair of people or things involved together, 'they' referring to a pair, 'different' in 'two men from different backgrounds', 'either side'.
- +1: neighboring tokens such as 'same', 'both', commas, 'everyone', 'crew'.

Negative values:
- −5 to −10: per-unit or distributive quantities. This covers 'each X for N Y', 'each party', 'N couples', 'N-bedroom' in a mix, repeated counts in itemized lists ('3 lunches, 3 dinners', '4 x forks'), and 'both' or 'every' applied to dates or intervals. The strongest value sits on the token that closes the distributive phrase (for example ')').
- −1 to −4: numbers in specifications or ranges ('20 characters', '(3″)', model ranges joined by 'and'), 'of' in 'sets of' or 'any of', and newlines in lists.

What does not fire:
- Plain plurals with no group or count framing.
- Ordinary numbers in addresses or dates without a distributive sense.
- General text.

expl.label: Computing/software-technical context (patent 'computer-readable storage medium'); negative: scholarly-insight phrasing
expl.positive_pole: Tokens in computing/software/digital-technology contexts, especially noun phrases describing software, storage, memory or hardware. The strongest case is the patent-claim boilerplate 'The computer-readable storage medium of claim…', where the peak falls on '-readable' (+10). Nearby tokens are also high: 'computer' (+6), 'storage'/'medium' (+7), 'The' (+4), 'of' (+3), and the claim number/period (+2). Weaker hits: 'software' in 'software-based' or 'software stored in' (+2 to +3), 'memory' or 'heap' when discussing programming (+1 to +2), and 'GPU', 'Implementation', 'machines', 'programming', 'Internet', 'file on his computer' (about +1).
expl.negative_pole: Academic, literary or humanistic evaluative phrasing about a work giving insight into a subject. Typical frames are 'of first importance in dealing with', 'an amazing insight into', 'a valuable lesson in', 'a view of', 'glimpse into', 'commentary on', 'hereinafter referred to as', and 'medieval history'. The activation lands on prepositions and function words that link the work to its subject ('into', 'with', 'in', 'of', 'as', commas). Typical values are -1 to -3; the peak is -7 on 'with' in 'dealing with'.
expl.rubric: Background is 0 for almost all tokens; the neuron is extremely sparse (|v|>=1 on about 0.01% of tokens). Positive rules: 'computer-readable storage medium' in patent-claim style gives +6 to +10, with the peak on '-readable' and about +7 on storage/medium. Other dense software/hardware/storage terminology in a technical description ('software-based', 'software stored in persistent memory', 'memory given to', 'parallel implementation', 'GPU computing') gives +1 to +3 on the technical noun or adjacent word. Casual mentions of tech such as TV, Internet or software tools give about +1 or often 0. Negative rules: in book or scholarship reviews with phrases like 'insight into', 'importance in dealing with', 'lesson in how', 'window into... a view of', assign -1 to -3 on the linking preposition or comma. Give up to about -7 only for a strong cumulative scholarly-evaluative frame such as 'of first importance in dealing with'. Surrounding words in that phrase get about -1. Ordinary narrative, nature, or commercial text gets 0. Non-technical uses of 'medium' or 'storage' should not fire strongly.

expl.label: Termination/endpoint condition of an ongoing process (until, as long as, stops)
expl.positive_pole: Tokens that introduce or complete the stopping condition of an ongoing activity, i.e. the point at which something ends. The strongest trigger is the connector itself: 'until' ('bake 15–18 minutes or until tops are firm', 'contest will continue until', 'repeating until Saturday', 'runs until 20.'), the 'as' of 'as long as' / 'as long as needed', and 'if' in 'taste to see if'. Words naming cessation also fire: 'Termination', 'stopping', 'stop', 'leave the tent', 'how long is desirable to keep'. The punctuation or end word that closes a completion condition fires too: the comma after 'check the fire was fully out,', '...the itch is still there to play,', 'clean' in 'toothpick comes out clean', the period after 'jiggly in the middle.'. In recipes, 'or' in 'X minutes or until' and the doneness word ('desired', 'set') get moderate activation.
expl.negative_pole: Tokens specifying a time schedule, interval, starting point or progress milestone rather than an end condition. Examples: '.\n' after 'Turn it over after 12 hours' (−8), 'work' in 'it would work' (−7), 'every 5 min' ('min' −6, the space before the number −5), 'reach your' in 'until you reach your normal regimen' (−6), 'start at' (−4/−5), 'about 2 cups' (−5), 'save-and-resume' (−5), '3 days on, 3 days off' (−4), 'and then' (−4), 'by the time you retire' (−4), 'the event' (−4), 'stirring' (−4). The pattern is periodic or step timing and the onset or reaching of a state, rather than ceasing.
expl.rubric: Background is about 0 on most tokens; scattered ±1 values are common on nearby content words. Assign these positive values: 'until' introducing an end condition +6 to +9; 'as' in 'as long as' +7 to +8; the comma or period that closes a completion clause ('fully out,', 'in the middle.') +7 to +10; 'Termination' +8; 'stopping'/'to stop' +5 to +7; recipe doneness words ('clean', 'set', 'desired') +3 to +7; preceding 'or'/'minutes' +2 to +4; words just after 'until' +1 to +3. Plain 'until' with no process-ending sense, such as 'until you reach X', may go slightly negative. Assign these negative values: schedule or interval specifics ('every 5 min', 'after 12 hours.', 'start at', 'X days on, Y off') −3 to −8; milestone or progress words ('reach', 'about 2 cups', 'by the time') −3 to −6. Ordinary prose stays near 0.

expl.label: Opening topic sentence of a new text body (+); mid-discourse we/you/the subjects (−)
expl.positive_pole: Tokens in the first sentence or clause of a fresh piece of prose that comes right after boilerplate such as a header, address, dateline, byline, citation or title. This is the expository, encyclopedic or promotional 'topic sentence' that introduces what the text is about. The activation peaks a few tokens in, on the main verb or predicate head and its first complement, then decays across the clause. Examples: 'Strip| away|+7'; 'Maritime archaeology| deals|+5 with|+4'; 'Today|+7,'; 'Animal lovers|+7 from'; 'is dedicated|+7 to|+3'; 'is making its mark|+7'; 'The|+7 qualitative exploration of|+5'; 'As a young child we|+7 dug'; 'mission of the ... Office is to fulfill|+7'; 'aims to provide a safe working environment|+6'; 'was raised|+6 by'; 'gives|+6 you the power|+4'; 'Spring is|+6 such|+5'; 'Ford Gallery is a|+6 contemporary art gallery|+4 in|+5'. A weaker version fires on descriptive or definitional predicate content elsewhere: 'X is/are...', 'of', 'for', 'to', abstract nouns like 'omnipresence|+6', 'hurtful|+6', '-esque|+6', 'rates|+5 ... have|+6'.
expl.negative_pole: Sharp single-token spikes on discourse-continuation subjects deep inside conversational, narrative or news prose. These are mostly the pronouns 'we' and 'you', plus sentence- or clause-initial 'the'/'This' that follows an earlier sentence. Examples: 'would| you|-10'; 'In the year ahead, we|-9 plan'; 'ensuring the|-9 big picture'; 'reason to be concerned that the|-9 next president'; '. This|-9 work was undertaken'; 'And we|-8 are making'; 'that we|-8 were'; 'I|-5 will make'. Odd mid-token spikes also occur, such as 'high‐|-10alkali' and 'Jan.|-8'. Mild negatives of −1 to −3 appear on digits in dates, zip codes and phone numbers, on citation/metadata tokens, on proper names in datelines, and on newlines in boilerplate.
expl.rubric:
Background: most tokens sit between −1 and +1; numerals and metadata typically −1 to −2.

Positive scoring:
- Fresh opening sentence of a body text right after header/address/date/byline: score its 2nd–5th tokens +5 to +7, usually the main verb, copula + complement head, or a sentence-initial 'Today'/'The'.
- The following function words in that clause (to, of, in, with, for, a): +2 to +4.
- Descriptive or definitional clauses mid-text ('X is dedicated to', 'aims to provide', 'rates in ... have'): +2 to +5.
- Ordinary words inside such clauses: +1 to +3.

Negative scoring:
- 'we' or 'you' as subject of a later sentence in chatty, editorial or narrative prose (e.g. 'we plan', 'would you', 'And we are'): −6 to −10.
- 'the' or 'This' starting a noun phrase after a mid-discourse clause boundary ('ensuring the', 'that the next', '. This work'): −5 to −9.
- 'I' as subject: −2 to −5.
- Pronouns 'you/it/his' elsewhere in conversational text: −1 to −3.

Does NOT fire:
- The header, address or date tokens themselves, which are slightly negative.
- Pronouns 'we' or 'you' when they open a fresh text, e.g. 'As a young child we dug', which is positive.

expl.label: Third-party testimonial/review attribution (−) vs. author's own first-person forum voice (+)
expl.positive_pole: Weak (usually +1 to +3). Fires in informal user-generated posts where the writer speaks in their own voice. It lands on the tokens that start or continue a first-person statement or question: "I", "we have", "can anyone", "should i", "dont", "That said, I". It favours sentence-initial tokens right after a period or newline. It also fires on post metadata such as "Posted on Oct 02, 2009", "Join Date: Jul 2004" and "Subscribe↵", with the digits of the year getting +1 to +3. Typical sites are forum help requests, blog asides and fan bios.
expl.negative_pole: Strong (down to −10). Fires where text attributes opinions or experiences to other people, as in reviews, testimonials, owner reports and user submissions. The largest values land on the noun naming the third-party group: "Some owners find" (−10 on "owners"), "Owners note" (−4), "used by a customer" (−4), "a KDE Plasma user" (−5 on "user"). Attribution frames also fire: "Submitted by NAME", "From: Tanner:", "Comments:", "Customer Raves & Reviews", "u/llorca336 gave", "feedback from", "delegates had to say", "we're chiming in", "Chapter will hold". The first token of the quoted testimonial that follows is also strongly negative: "I" or "“I" (−5 to −6), ""This" (−5), and "!↵" ending a review (−5). Usernames and the newlines in these attribution lines get −1 to −3.
expl.rubric: Background is 0 for most text, including ordinary narrative, news and technical prose. Score the negative pole as follows. A noun naming a group of other people whose views or experiences are reported (owners, customers, users, reviewers, delegates) scores −4 to −10, strongest for generalizations like "Some owners find". The token opening a quoted review or testimonial scores −3 to −6. Attribution labels such as "Submitted by", "From:", "Comments:", "Reviews" and "feedback from", plus the username tokens after them, score −1 to −3. Score the positive pole as follows. In an informal first-person forum or blog post, the sentence-initial "I" or "We" or a question opener scores +1 to +3. The dates and years in post timestamps or join-date headers score +1 to +3. Surrounding function words in those sentences score +1. Positive values rarely exceed +3. First-person "I" inside a quoted customer testimonial is NEGATIVE, not positive; the key cue is a review or attribution context.

expl.label: Word-prefix fragment awaiting completion (+) vs. standalone abbreviation (-)
expl.positive_pole: Fires on a token that is the opening fragment of a longer word the model expects to continue, mid-word, usually a proper noun or technical term whose completion is highly predictable. Examples: Princeton «Rep»(ertory), PH«IL»(HARMONIC), «mass»(achusetts), 1 «Th»«ess»(alonians), «FL»(ORIDA), «Cab»(ernet), Les «Mis»(érables), Eagle-T«rib»(une), «breast»(stroke), RUSSIAN F«ED»(ERATION), «rh»(inoceros), «pot»(entiometer), Army «Pam»(phlet), Trans-«App»(alachian), «Ob»«it»(uary), re«trans»(mission). Usually the first sub-token carries the peak. A second fragment can also fire (Th +7, ess +9). The remaining continuation tokens of the word get weaker values (+1 to +3) or none.
expl.negative_pole: Short tokens, often capitalized, that are complete abbreviations or acronyms standing alone, where the word is finished rather than continuing. Examples: LR (living room) -6, SS (stainless steel) -4, PD/AD (diseases) -3 to -4, NC -4, OO (object-oriented) -4, cu. in. -4/-3, Ss (subjects) -4, PK -3, St. -3, Co. -3, pic -3, elec -3. Mild negatives (about -1) appear on some name or word fragments in ambiguous contexts.
expl.rubric: Background is 0 for nearly all tokens, including ordinary whole words. Assign +7 to +10 when a token is the clear beginning of a multi-token word with a strongly predictable completion: famous names, place names, book names, wine grapes, technical nouns. Assign +3 to +5 for word-initial fragments of less predictable or common technical words (tux, mal, sulfas-al, Em-ulators, polysty-rene, mac & cheese). Assign +1 to +2 for weak or generic fragments (Sub-s, photojournal-ist, Zoro-astrian, Neb.). Later sub-tokens of the same word get 0 to +3. Assign -3 to -6 to a standalone uppercase or short abbreviation that is complete in itself, particularly in listings, real-estate, medical or technical text. Abbreviations that are actually word-starts (FL→ORIDA, IN in an address) count as positive, because the model reads them as continuing or state-like. Full words and punctuation get about 0.

expl.label: Ongoing/completing processes (conversion, download, dissolving), esp. awaiting completion
expl.positive_pole: Tokens naming or describing a process that runs over time and reaches completion, usually in instructional or technical text where a later step waits on it. Examples: software operations (export request, conversion, download, transfer, import, restore, booting, printing queue, installation), cooking steps that run until done (until dissolved, until liquid is absorbed, add eggs one at a time, sugar dissolves), and devices or other things running (water running, charging program, garage door closing). The strongest firing is on the process noun or the completion predicate inside 'once/after/when the X is finished/complete' and 'click Start to start the conversion' frames.
expl.negative_pole: Weak and diffuse, never below about -1.6. Mild negatives (-1 to -2) fall on UI or keyboard objects and nouns in instructions: Print Screen hotkey, 'press', button, shopping cart, sound, flour. These are not semantically coherent and can be treated as essentially background.
expl.rubric:
Background is 0 on almost all tokens.
- +10: a process noun in a technical command or request, e.g. 'Request' in 'New-MailboxExportRequest' (+10), with 'Export' at about +5.
- +4 to +7: the process noun or completion verb in a completion frame. Examples: 'the conversion process has been completed' (conversion +7, process +6, completed +4); 'when your computer is finished booting' (finished +6); 'start the conversion' (start +6); 'transfer client' (transfer +6); 'operation is' (+5); 'once the import is finished' (is +5, finished +4); 'until liquid is absorbed' (liquid +5).
- +1 to +4: surrounding tokens in these frames ('the', 'is', 'complete', 'download', 'dissolved', 'one at a time', 'water running', 'charging', 'order', 'Copy', 'transcode').
- Anchor phrases: 'once/after/when ... is complete/finished', 'until ... dissolved/absorbed', and 'process/operation/download/installation'.
- Ordinary narrative, descriptive or opinion text stays at 0.
- Instruction-UI nouns may reach -1 occasionally.

expl.label: Product care/operation instructions (+) vs. build/produce/re-do capability claims (−)
expl.positive_pole: Text that instructs or explains how a product or device is physically treated or operated. Typical cases are garment care labels ("Machine wash cold, gentle cycle, do not tumble dry", "wash at 40°", "pre-washed for softness"), device mechanisms ("uses ultrasonic technology to deliver a safe, heat-free mist", "the nicotine vaporizes the…", "turntable motor unit", "reads the very center") and step-by-step run/install directions ("run the exe application", "run the game as administrator as it helps prevent crashes", "burning the DSL image to a CD-R", "double-click", "running under OS 9"). Activation lands on the key process or condition words: washed, cold, spin, heat, 40, CD, vaporizes, run, administrator, and the 'it' in 'as it helps'. The function words that continue the instruction also fire (for, to, the, and).
expl.negative_pole: Statements about what can be built, produced, regenerated or redone, usually in software, build or fabrication contexts. Examples: "recompiled in a stable environment", "edit them to remove… and re-", "you can build them via knobs", "…voila… you get a dataset", "run it against different configurations", "can also be uploaded", "easier to slice as everything is done", "capable of printing up to", "pre-cut a 3D model in hundreds of shards in seconds", "customers will be able to have their name", "recording directly to executable test". The peak falls on the re- prefix, the outcome pronoun ('you' get, 'it' against), modal or infinitive words ('be', 'to', 'of', 'in') before the produced result or quantity, and on build/slice/done verbs. Words about 3D printing or printing often sit around −1 to −4.
expl.rubric: Background is 0 for most tokens; ordinary prose drifts around ±1 on scattered function words. Garment care-instruction words: +3 to +6, rising to +6–10 for the decisive word (washed, cold, 40°, spin, tumble). Device mechanism or how-it-works phrases: +3–9 on the key word (heat, vaporizes, turn[table]). Software run/install steps: +3–8 (run, exe, CD, 'it helps'). Words like to/for/the inside such instructions: +1–4. Product spec lists such as fabric percentages: +1–5. Negative side: build/produce/redo capability phrasing in software, packaging or 3D-printing text scores −3 to −9. The re- prefix of recompiled/re-release reaches −8 to −9, and the 'you' in 'you get a dataset' about −8. 'be able to', 'capable of', 'in seconds' and 'up to N' score −4 to −7. Generic mentions of software or printing without instructional or capability framing stay near 0 to −2. Marketing or narrative text with no procedure stays near 0.

expl.label: Restating the addressee's given facts (+) vs. hypothetical or unknown conditions (−)
expl.positive_pole: Tokens inside a clause that echoes information the addressee or user has already supplied, used as a known premise for a reply or inference. Typical frames: "since you are flying to Paris on TAM", "since you said", "(you in this scenario)", "What you say you're looking for is", "you have opted to", "You are searching for", "as is your requirement", "Detail provided for", "The part \"...\" of the query". Activation peaks on the verb, preposition or noun that completes the stated premise, just before the new content or conclusion: on (+10), are (+7), scenario (+7), is (+7), have (+7), searching (+6), said (+5), requirement (+5). It weakly generalizes to any given or specified parameter being anchored: "at boot", "at a price point of", "when the snow begins", "hit only once", "actually 0,67", "for your smaller gathering".
expl.negative_pole: Hypothetical, conditional or unknown situations, where the speaker reasons about something not given or poses a what-if or diagnostic question. Examples: "How about 27" (about, −8), "if you turn this to just air, does the fan..." (does, −7), "where it mounts" (where, −6), "without seeing what" (what, −6), "you might be having" (having, −5), "if he simply uses" (uses, −5), "You didn't say what type of medication she is on" (on, −5), "If it is built in" (is, −5; in, −4), "If I have kids," (comma, −4), "he might look like" (like, −4), "describe it as" (as, −4). The activation falls on the verb, wh-word or preposition right after the conditional, modal or question frame.
expl.rubric: Background is 0 for nearly all tokens; scattered ±1 noise on ordinary prose is common, e.g. −1 on news nouns and prepositions. Score +5 to +10 only when the text explicitly restates what "you" (the reader, user or questioner) said, chose, is doing or requires, and uses it as a premise; put the peak on the completing token (verb, preposition or object) right before the conclusion. The connective tokens "since", "but" and "you" get +1 to +2, and the next token after the peak often gets +1 to +3. Score +2 to +5 for given specifications or parameters such as "Detail provided for", "at boot", "price point of", "held on", "found at http". Score −3 to −8 for hypothetical, conditional or unknown-condition reasoning: tokens right after if, might, how about, without seeing what, or does in a diagnostic question. Plain mentions of "you" without restating given info score about 0, and plain narrative scores about 0. Large magnitudes on either pole are rare.

expl.label: End of a parallel list item / repeated-pattern slot in enumerations
expl.positive_pole: Tokens inside coordinated lists and repeated parallel structures, usually the 2nd, 3rd or later items. It fires most on the last token of an item that mirrors an earlier item's form, and on the separator (comma, 'and', 'or') right after that item, which sets up another parallel item. Examples: 'English, French«,»' in a language list; 'red deer «and» pigs«,»'; 'a finch «or» canary'; 'Alcott«,» Annehurst«,» and'; '/home/username-two/xyz«.com»' after an identical first path; 'F – 5 would be the camera «sticker»' echoing 'the Dart board sticker'; '3 suit «game»'; 'Joel Ros«ario», 20-1' in a results list; 'Washington«,» D.C.' at the end of a list of companies and cities; 'other types of «businesses»'. The neuron rises as the parallelism builds up.
expl.negative_pole: Weak, at most about -4. It appears where text leaves a list or name and moves into a predicate or clause continuation. Examples: 'The procedure for the right «is identical»'; 'And «the» market does…'; 'knew «it» paired'; 'Monkey Town… «has» spread'; 'Does anyone remember «that»'; 'for the second «time»'; inside long proper-name strings such as 'Sik«ors»ky' or 'El «Caj»on'. Also seen at a newline that ends a list line before a non-parallel line.
expl.rubric:
Background is 0 for most prose tokens. In a list or enumeration:
- First item: about 0-1.
- Later items and their separators: +1 to +4.
- Peak, at the head/end token or comma of a clearly parallel later item, especially when the list is long or the pattern repeats exactly: +5 to +10.
- Words within an item: small values (+1 to +3), with the highest value on the item's final token or the delimiter after it.
- Tables and results lists (names, numbers, ' |' separators): moderate to high, +3 to +8.
- Single non-list prose, even with commas or 'and' joining clauses: about 0 to +1.
- Verbs and determiners that start a predicate right after a list or name: -1 to -4, typically -1 to -2.

expl.label: Distinguishing modifier in 'X is just Y, only different' reframings
expl.positive_pole: Deflationary or reframing statements that recast something as the same familiar thing differing only in one respect: 'just a really long one', 'little kids in bigger bodies', 'just have to get used to a new way of dialing', 'merely new expressions of', 'in another way', 'looking in different directions', 'I just never knew it', 'just a really expensive door stop', 'works the same, but instead of...'. Activation sits on the tokens that state the difference (new, different, another, bigger, really, way, instead, with, slightly differing) and on the hedges that set up the frame (just, merely, albeit). It is strongest on the head of the difference phrase, e.g. 'way' in 'new way', 'bigger' in 'in bigger bodies', 'really' in 'just a really long one'.
expl.negative_pole: Negligible, about -1 at most. Weak negatives fall on plain contrast or categorical nouns in expository, legal or business text, e.g. 'every sub-type is different', 'statute of limitations', 'one class of stock', 'sui generis'. These involve no 'same thing, slight variation' framing.
expl.rubric: Background is 0 on almost all tokens. Assign +6 to +10 to the key difference word in a clear 'it's just X, but [new/bigger/different/really long]' reframe ('way' in 'a new way of dialing' = 10; 'bigger' = 9; 'really' in 'just a really long one' = 9; 'just' in 'I just never knew it' = 8; 'different directions' = 7; 'another way' = 6). Give +2 to +5 to nearby words in the same frame ('just', 'to get used to', 'albeit', 'merely', 'expressions', 'one', 'of') and to weaker same-but-different cases ('identical but with different capacities' = 3; 'slightly differing approaches and nuances' = 2-4; 'works the same, but instead' = 3-4; 'more delicate elaborations' = 4). Give +1 to +2 to loosely related comparative or 'just' phrasings. Plain uses of 'different', 'new' or 'just' with no reframing of a familiar thing get 0. Minor -1 goes on dry technical nouns or flat contrastive statements.

expl.label: Positive on modifiers before a re-mentioned noun; negative on referent heads
expl.positive_pole: Fires on the token just before a head word that is predictable from earlier context, usually because it re-mentions something already discussed. Typical carriers are possessors, determiners, adjectives and fixed-phrase starters. Examples: "Apple|'s" (helper = the Siri already discussed), "jurisdiction|al" (puzzles, mentioned earlier), "these|types" (of presses), "SolarWorld|'s" (capacity), "monthly" (nut, repeated), "THUMBS-D|OWN" (mirrors THUMBS-UP), "of|ozone" (destruction, repeated), "% Daily|Value", "with" (respect to), "Pujols' former trainer|," just before the name. Also fires on a link verb or relativizer introducing info about a known entity: "The deceased|is", "the President, |who", "counsel|is".
expl.negative_pole: Fires on the head itself: the noun or pronoun that refers back to an already-established entity, especially as subject or object inside a clause. Examples: "sending|them" (=friends) -10, "the velocity|vector" -10/-6, "in|my" -10, "per migrant|worker" -9, "coached by|him since|they|were" -4/-8/-4, "the|child|'s" -8, "the|parameter" -8, "PNL|is|the" -7/-4, "single grits,|tool" -7, "When|he" -7, "which|he", "which|has" -6.
expl.rubric: Background is ~0, with scattered ±1 on ordinary content words. Positive scores: +5 to +9 for a possessive 's, adjective suffix, determiner or connector right before a head noun that echoes earlier context (e.g. "Apple's" +8, "jurisdictional" +8, "with respect" +9). Give +2 to +4 when the echo is weaker or the phrase is merely formulaic. Negative scores: -6 to -10 for a pronoun or noun head that is the re-mentioned referent, especially an object or subject pronoun after a verb or preposition ("them", "him", "he", "they", "my"). The same applies to a repeated technical noun head ("velocity", "parameter", "worker", "tool", "child"), and to "is"/"has" right after a topic entity or "which". Give -2 to -4 for weaker cases. First mentions of new entities, and generic function words with no back-reference, get ~0.

expl.label: Beneficial outcomes/payoffs: 'benefits', 'save', 'advantage', 'solve', 'reduce'
expl.positive_pole: Words that name the positive payoff, value or result of using something, in promotional or evaluative text. The main triggers are 'benefit(s)', 'advantage', 'save', 'solve', 'reduce/lower', 'realize (success)', 'results ... seen' and 'savings'. The peak lands on the payoff word itself. Activation is strongest when the context sets up an expectation of a benefit, as in 'what are the benefits of', 'the advantage of X is that', 'save up to 90%', 'more problems than they solve', 'further facilitate the above mentioned benefits' and 'can save money by'. Tokens right after the payoff word also get moderate activation, e.g. 'of', 'to', 'by', 'that', '%', the '?' after 'advantage'. So do framing words just before it, such as 'the', 'great', 'several', 'further', 'save up to'.
expl.negative_pole: Weak, at most about -2.4, and diffuse. It shows up on neutral or negative cost, burden and spec-measurement nouns: 'impact' in an environmental LCA sense, 'insurance', 'power' needed, 'response' time, 'noise', 'loud'. It also hits some function words in non-benefit contexts ('for', 'to', 'the'). Treat it as near zero except for small negatives of about -1 to -2 on such cost, measure or problem nouns.
expl.rubric:
Background is 0 on almost all tokens; about 99.8% of tokens are below 1. Scoring:
- +5 to +10: the head payoff word in a clear benefit frame, e.g. 'solve' in 'more problems than they solve' = 10; 'benefits' in 'the above mentioned benefits' = 9; 'benefits'/'advantage'/'save'/'reduce'/'lower' in a benefit question or claim = 5-7.
- +2 to +4: words directly attached to the payoff, such as 'of'/'to'/'by'/'that' after 'benefits/advantage', 'to' in 'save up to', '%' in a savings figure, 'money' after 'save', 'they' before 'solve', 'great' in 'great benefits/great way'. Also lone weaker value words: 'savings', 'objectives', 'compared to', 'several ... benefits'.
- +1: nearby promotional framing, e.g. 'cost-effective', 'improve', 'offers', 'leverage', 'why should you choose', 'free services'.
- Plain mentions of 'impact', 'features' and 'results' without a payoff frame get only 0-1.
- Negative: -1 to -2 on cost, requirement or measurement nouns ('insurance', 'power', 'response time', 'environmental impact', 'noise'); otherwise 0.
- 'benefit' as an employment fringe benefit, or in negative or neutral statistics contexts, stays low.

expl.label: Technological/historical progress: things now easier, cheaper, more available than before
expl.positive_pole: Narratives of change over time toward improvement, availability or modernity. Typical frames: 'X is now far easier', 'more effective medications', 'lower turbine prices', 'reduction in costs', 'availability of fMRI data', 'treatments we have available are much more effective', 'now responsive', 'before they were even cool', 'yet to be seen', 'one day we'll actually have viable…'. The peak lands on the comparative or progress word ('easier', 'more', 'prices', 'costs', 'available', 'current', 'new', 'now') right after a temporal or comparative cue ('now far', 'are developing', 'lower', 'in recent years the').
expl.negative_pole: Weak, max about -5. Fires on a user's current or existing possession, or the setup they are switching from. Examples: 'from your current network', 'products he currently has', 'I don't have time', 'already had the equipment', 'my current order fulfillment', 'move away from Shopify', 'Upgrading your Operating System', 'Illustrator version', 'price range'. These are consumer or tech-support contexts about switching, choosing or upgrading. The negative lands on the possession or noun token ('current', 'has', 'equipment', 'Shopify', 'version').
expl.rubric: Background is 0 on almost all tokens. Assign +8 to +10 to the key progress word in an explicit 'now much easier / more effective / lower prices' statement about advancement. Assign +5 to +7 to nearby supporting words or to milder cases: 'availability of', 'current level of sophistication', 'all the new', 'now used instead', 'is now one step closer', 'wish there was'. Assign +2 to +4 to surrounding function words in the phrase ('to', 'by', 'and', 'of', 'have'), to anticipation of improvement ('hopeful for improvement in final products', 'can't wait until better'), and to historical framing ('since the first … in 2004', 'as it used to be'). Give +1 to weak temporal cues ('Today,', 'decades ago', 'recently'). Assign -1 to -3 in switching or upgrade discussions where the speaker refers to their current or existing item, rising to about -5 on 'current' in 'your current network'. Plain technical, scientific or narrative text without a time-improvement framing stays at 0.

expl.label: Location/place reference where something stands, fills, or replaces (site, where, in place of)
expl.positive_pole: Tokens that name or point to a physical or abstract location as the spot where something exists, stands, is put, or substitutes for something else. The biggest peak is on the head noun 'site' in phrases like 'the trade center site' or 'at the site' (+7 to +10). 'where'/'wherever' clauses fire on 'where' and on the following existential verb or article ('where there is a well', 'where the webcam would normally be'). Substitution frames fire on 'in place of', 'in its place a', and 'replace'. Location-filling verbs fire too: 'filled that house', 'stood on what had been a', 'now stands', 'leaving only', 'fill in imperfections'. Other spatial nouns such as spot, ground, pit, and center also count. Activation often peaks on the token that completes the locative slot ('site', 'ground', 'be', 'would', 'stands', 'a' after 'had been'/'there is').
expl.negative_pole: Weak, only down to about -3. It fires on product and marketing gift language: 'makes a perfect gift', 'an ideal gift for any occasion', 'addition to any home', 'your needs', 'on the go', 'everyday life'. The most negative tokens are usually 'a', 'gift', 'any', or 'your' in these sales clichés, typically -1 to -3.
expl.rubric:
Background is 0 for almost all tokens.
- +7 to +10: the locative head of a 'where something stands/is built' context, e.g. 'site' in 'the trade center site' or 'at the site', 'ground' in 'the dry ground', 'would' in 'where the dark would', 'a' in 'what had been a'.
- +4 to +7: 'in place of' / 'in its place' (on 'place' and 'of'); 'where' or 'wherever' followed by 'there is a' or 'X are/is/be'; 'spot' in 'in that spot'; 'now stands'; 'replace'; 'filled that'; 'pit of'.
- +2 to +4: 'leaving only/just', 'fill in', 'in the', 'out of thin air', 'wherever a ... is', and generic 'site' or 'place' mentions.
- +1: weak spatial words such as 'places', 'water', 'substitute', 'placeholder', 'somewhere'.
- Does NOT fire: plain 'site' meaning website, or 'where' used as a non-locative relative. Expect only small values for these.
- Negative: -1 to -3 on gift/marketing phrases like 'makes a perfect gift for', 'any home', 'your needs'.

expl.label: Competition results: negative for wins/titles/awards, positive for performance/qualifying details
expl.positive_pole: Weak, diffuse positive activation in competitive or evaluative contexts that describe performance, qualification or meeting criteria rather than winning outright. Examples: 'met' in 'homes that met our requirements' (+5); 'only' in 'leaves Hoffman as only' (+4); 'runs' and 'Seed Time' with times like '7.77' (+2 to +4); 'test', 'able', 'drivers', 'solution', 'advancing', 'safety'. It tends to land on the verb or noun that sets up the measured result, or on the digits of a time or score.
expl.negative_pole: Strong activation on tokens that name a victory, championship, award or top ranking that someone won or holds. It peaks on the title or prize noun: 'championship' in 'wins second straight XTERRA championship' (-10); 'MVP' in 'NL MVP honors' (-9); 'wins' (-7); 'Premier League' (-7); 'Year' in 'Designer of the Year' (-6); 'Award' (-3); 'number-one position' (-4). It also fires on the years or ordinals attached to wins ('wins in 1962, 1970' → -4 to -7 on the digits; 'his 20th anniversary' → -9 on '0'). Function words in these phrases also fire: 'the', 'of', 'for', ',' and 'in' around the prize get -2 to -6.
expl.rubric:
Background is 0 almost everywhere; ordinary text, ads and non-competitive prose stay below 0.5.

Negative scale:
- Explicit win/award/title phrases, on the prize noun: -6 to -10 ('championship', 'MVP', 'title', 'Oscar ... win', 'of the Year').
- Verbs like won/wins/dominated/named and nearby function words or years: -2 to -7.
- Milder honors such as 'Innovation Award', 'winner of', 'number-one' or 'Premier Performer': -2 to -4.

Positive scale:
- Sports or competition reports that give times, seeds, runs or participation details: +1 to +4 on the numbers and setup words.
- Criteria-meeting or qualification phrases ('met our requirements', 'only team to have beaten', 'able to', 'top five were able'): +3 to +5 on the key verb or quantifier.
- Most positive values are +1 to +2.

Distinction: actually winning or receiving an award goes negative. Competing, measured performance, ranks short of victory, or meeting conditions go mildly positive. Ordinal places like 'fourth' or 'second' are often slightly negative (-1).

expl.label: Diffuse neuron for formulaic boilerplate phrases (positive) versus clause-joining words (negative)
expl.positive_pole:
Tokens inside stock, highly predictable phrases, where the continuation is nearly fixed. Typical sources are web boilerplate and set formulas:
- "By using our websites,"
- "Your continued use of"
- "By clicking AGREE … you confirm"
- "receive notifications of new posts by email"
- "Get every new post delivered to your Inbox"
- "Click Here To Check Price"
- "custom writing services"
- "Forward-looking statements are"
- "on your behalf"
- "appeared to be impaired" (police-report style)
- "take away the sins of many" (scripture)
- year ranges like "from 2007 to 2012" (the year digit after "20" and the word "to" fire)

The peak lands on the word that commits to or continues the template, such as "use", "confirm", "receive", "delivered", "services", "to", the year digit, or a comma after a fixed opener. It also fires on SEO/spam product or marketing slogans ("Be stylish", "binary options") and on transliterated name or keyword fragments in spam ("Daiichi", "slubna gdansk").
expl.negative_pole:
Function words and punctuation that join or pivot clauses in generic, often SEO-spun or promotional/news prose. Examples:
- the comma in "essay with skills, so far" (-10)
- "our" in "fired at one of our members" (-9)
- "now" in "You now have some knowledge" (-8)
- "find" in "You can find a few ladies" (-8)
- "allows" in "Personal Information … allows us" (-7)
- "with" in "along with your buyer" (-7)
- the comma in "so, too, will" (-7)
- "&" in "United States & the" (-7)
- "are" in "Following are Major" (-7)
- "to" in "improvements to be reported" (-7)
- units after numbers, e.g. "mm" in "415mm" (-8)
- foreign words such as "Sämtliche" (-8)

Weak -1 to -2 is common on digits within numbers and dates, on color/descriptive adjectives, and on proper-name pieces.
expl.rubric:
Background:
- Most tokens are 0.
- About 12% of tokens sit at ±1. Expect mild +1 on function words in flowing prose and -1 on number digits, names, and descriptive nouns.
- Strong values are rare: |value| ≥3 on only about 0.05% of tokens.

Positive values:
- +5 to +10: the committing token of a well-known boilerplate or formula. Examples are "Your continued use", "By clicking … you confirm", "receive notifications", "delivered to your Inbox", and the year digits and "to" in "from 2007 to 2012".
- +2 to +4: nearby words within the same formula, e.g. "of", "by", "email", "your".

Negative values:
- -5 to -10: occasional, hard to predict. Usually a clause-linking function word, pronoun, or comma in spun or marketing text where the sentence pivots ("allows us", "along with", "so, too", "You now have", "can find").
- -2 to -4: next to such pivots.

What does not fire:
- Ordinary narrative or technical prose stays within ±1.
- Isolated numbers stay at about -1 unless they are part of a 'from YEAR to YEAR' formula.

expl.label: Sparse, polysemantic: fires at the last token of set phrases or names
expl.positive_pole: Fires on the token that finishes a familiar multi-token unit. Examples: the title word that closes a known name ("All Is Well" peaks on "Well", +10); a head noun after a modifier ("generic version" +7, "longtime companion" +4, "any extras" +4, "boom beach" +4); and inner digits of phone numbers or quantities ("21"1 +4, "162"→"2" +4, "750" on "5" +4). It also fires weakly on function words that come right after a clause or subject ("calling it" +5, "sequences at" +4, "Savings and" +4, "they had" +4, "This product" +3–4). There is no single clear semantic theme.
expl.negative_pole: Fires on the token that completes a compound, name or number. Examples: "one-and-done" (on "done", -9); a digit inside a number in a URL or product code ("1500" → "0", -9; "MR2" -7); the surname in "Bill Cunningham" (-8). Other cases: dice or stat digits ("+1" -7, "18 d" -6, "1.25" -5), and phrase-final nouns or adverbs such as "future rates" -5, "reds" -5, "diamond cut" -5, "just as" -4, "whole lot" -4, "small measure" -3, "grape" -3. Negatives tend to involve completions that are more lexicalized or compound-like than the positive ones.
expl.rubric: Background is 0 on nearly every token; about 0.4% of tokens reach |value|≥1. Most activations are ±1, scattered on mid-phrase tokens, digits and names. Reserve |value|≥3 for a token that completes a tight multi-token unit (name, title, idiom, compound noun, or digit inside a number). Sign heuristics: use positive (+3 to +10) for the final word of a title or name, a noun after an adjective, or a function word right after a subject or verb. Use negative (-3 to -9) for the second half of hyphenated idioms, surnames after first names, digits inside codes, URLs or stat lines, and quantity idioms ("a whole lot", "small measure", "just as"). The first token of a unit is usually near 0. Ordinary prose stays at 0.

expl.label: Proud, celebratory affirmation of one's own group, place, faith or self
expl.positive_pole: Warm, promotional or devotional praise of an in-group or identity: one's nation, region, hometown, faith or self ('our country', 'Ireland's greatest treasure', 'proudly made in England', 'how God has always been', 'I like who I am', 'how much talent we have', 'beautiful languages,', 'the wonders of biomedicine'). Activation lands on the function or possessive token that completes the proud claim ('has', 'have', 'be', 'am', 'our', ''s', ',', 'to'), and also on the place/identity noun itself ('England', 'African', 'Indian', 'country', 'Africa') or on praise nouns ('pride', 'treasures', 'wonders').
expl.negative_pole: Matter-of-fact, journalistic (often news or sports) references to a collective entity's own possession, belonging or condition ('in their own conditions', 'on their home turf', 'it was all Big Horn', 'continue to belong to the same circuit', 'Japan is a signatory', 'the Jewish community', 'Georgia's democracy is', 'the nation's plunge', 'boost the share of', 'print our logo'). Peaks fall on possessive or determiner tokens ('their', 'the', 'to') and on the group or place name. These references are detached or evaluative rather than celebratory.
expl.rubric:
Background is about 0 for almost all tokens. Small ±1 flickers are common on function words.

Positive:
- +7 to +10: the climactic token of an explicit proud or affectionate in-group claim, e.g. 'has' in 'God has always been', 'have' in 'we have', 'be' in 'proud to be', 'our' in 'How cute is our', 'country' in 'brides of our country', ''s' in 'Ireland's greatest'.
- +3 to +6: surrounding praise words and place or identity names in promotional text ('proudly made in', 'greatest', 'treasures', 'deserves to be cherished', 'Indian army', 'Africa').
- +1 to +4: plain or brand mentions of a place or nation in promotional or neutral copy ('Survey of India', 'Cornwall', 'Flint Crepe', 'awesome!').

Negative:
- -3 to -6: possessive or determiner tokens in detached news or sports statements about a team, nation or community and its own home, rights or belonging ('their own', 'home turf', 'belong to', 'the Jewish community', 'Georgia's democracy').
- -1 to -3: a nation or team name in critical or neutral news ('Japan is', 'Green Bay', 'American astronauts').

The sign depends on tone and framing. Celebratory first-person or 'our' framing is positive. Neutral third-person reporting is negative. Generic positive adjectives with no in-group pride stay near 0 to +2.

expl.label: Positive: predictable mid-construction connectives/verbs; negative: repeated or parallel subject/list nouns
expl.positive_pole: Function words and light verbs sitting inside an ongoing, highly conventional multi-word construction, where the following words are strongly predictable. The token that carries the activation is the hinge or linking word of the frame. Examples: "as" in "as it crashes into"; "that" in "KNOWING that" or "a generally-accepted fact that"; "or" in "in whole or in part" and "customised or made to order"; "used up"; "as they relate to"; "weighs up a bid"; "trusting in God's"; "should be"; "versus"; "have a low"; "they say"; "suffering a"; "Leavy's crew". It often appears right after a subordinate "as/that/who + pronoun" opener, on the verb or the connective that follows. The hinge itself is high (6-10), and neighbouring tokens of the same phrase pick up a spread of +1 to +4.
expl.negative_pole:
Content nouns or names, plus some verbs, that repeat an entity already mentioned or fill a parallel slot in a list. These are often a subject or head noun just before or as the verb of a report or comparison. The negative usually lands on the head noun or verb right after the repeated name or parallel modifier, with smaller negatives on the following 1-2 tokens. Examples:
- "Kai's Cats" after Kai was already introduced
- "South Africa's" in a country list
- "Bangladeshi households" after "Black Caribbean households"
- "Sheriff's deputies say"
- "the researchers noted"
- "other galleries"
- "warm drinks" in a list of fluids
- "animals and plants survive"
- "Dearborn received" in a list of award winners
- "poke around"
- "when we provide"
- "the author Louis"
expl.rubric:
Background is about 0. Many tokens in ordinary prose sit at ±1, with mild +1 to +2 common on prepositions and articles inside verb phrases.
- +8 to +10: the connective or verb hinge of a stock frame ("in whole or", "KNOWING that", "as it", "customised or", "used up", "as they relate", "is about to").
- +4 to +7: similar but less idiomatic continuations ("they say", "weighs up", "trusting in", "should be", "suffering a", "posted a sign reading").
- +2 to +3: surrounding tokens of the same phrase.
- -8 to -10: the head noun or name in a repeated-entity or parallel-list slot, especially a subject before a reporting or action verb ("Kai", "Africa", "deputies", "researchers", "Bang", "received").
- -3 to -5: tokens immediately after that slot ("'s", "Cats", "drinks", "hi").
- Most nouns, names and punctuation stay near 0.

expl.label: Digits in lists of dates/numbers (+); time-unit words after numbers (−)
expl.positive_pole: Number tokens in repetitive, structured lists of dates, times, figures or stats, such as timestamp lines, news-feed dates, rankings with values, percentages, age lists and dimensions. The model is predicting the next digits. Activation lands on the digit or punctuation tokens inside the number, especially the leading digit after a space and the '0' in '20xx' years. It also lands on separators (',' ':' '-' 'x' '.') and on the month or weekday token that starts a repeated date entry. It is strongest when the same format has already appeared earlier, so the second and third entries in a list fire more than the first.
expl.negative_pole: Time and quantity unit words right after a number, especially in relative-time phrases: 'months' in '9 months ago', 'year', 'years', 'weeks', 'days', 'seconds', 'y'. The unit word carries the activation; 'ago' and the following comma are weaker. Similar but weaker effects occur on the last digit of a year in 'Net Worth in 2023' and on spaces or numbers in counting phrases ('five of its last six', '; 37 were').
expl.rubric: Background is 0 for nearly all prose. Positive values: +6 to +10 on a key digit or separator in repeated date or number list entries, e.g. 'Apr 26, 20|11' where '0' gets +8, the space before '14' after 'Japan', the ':' in '6:22', '.4' in '.40'. +2 to +5 on other digits, month names, weekday names and commas in such lists. +1 to +3 on an isolated date or number in prose, e.g. 'Nebraska, 4.0 percent' or 'with 0.5 seconds'. Negative values: −5 to −10 on 'months', 'years', 'year' in 'N months ago' or 'member for 2 years'. −3 to −5 on 'years old', 'seconds', 'days', 'weeks'. −1 to −3 on the surrounding 'ago', commas and counting words. Not firing: numbers inside normal sentences without list or format structure (near 0), and ordinary words.

expl.label: Vowelless consonant-cluster tokens (btw, srv, lb, vl, nd) → strongly negative
expl.positive_pole: Weak only, typically +1 to +2. It fires on subword pieces of rare or unusual names, acronyms and all-caps words that are split into pronounceable chunks containing vowels. Examples: Century, Ru(pees), J-AK-RO-SO-FT, PE PI, F.A.C.T, CAN-DE-LS, Son-far-rel, DIS-CI-PL-INE, sam-eness, Rout-ledge, Ost-bah-nhof, her-m-aph-rodite. It also fires faintly on a few ordinary tokens in boilerplate text (', and', 'Please', '$'). It looks like general 'odd fragmentary wordpiece that still has a vowel'.
expl.negative_pole: The dominant pole. It fires on short tokens made only of consonants (no vowels), usually lowercase, 2–3 letters. These appear as chat or text abbreviations, mangled or compressed words, URL fragments, or unusual name pieces. Strong examples: 'nd' in snd img (-10), 'vl' in dvlerner (-9), 'lb' in 'lbvs' (-8), 'lg' in mlgmxy (-8), 'bt' in 'btw' (-8), 'wt' in 'wtfff' (-7), 'srv' in 'srvices' (-7), 'pc' in spcanorth (-7), 'g' in Trgovich (-7), 'pl' in 'Cpl Group' (-7), 'BT' model code (-7), 'KB' in 'KBH Games' (-7). Uppercase consonant acronyms (TPB, KY, LW, GW, LX, NCLB, FPS, RX, tv, cd) are weaker, around -2 to -3. The token right after the cluster is often mildly negative (-1 to -2, e.g. 'w' after 'bt', 'img', 'm', 'H').
expl.rubric: Background is 0 for nearly all tokens, including normal English words. Assign -7 to -10 to a lowercase or mixed-case all-consonant token of 2–3 letters that sits inside a nonstandard word, abbreviation, username, URL or surname (btw, wtf, srv, snd, dvl, mlg, Trg, Cpl). Assign about -7 to model or brand codes in uppercase consonants (BT-023, KBH). Assign -2 to -4 to uppercase all-consonant acronyms in ordinary prose (TPB, NCLB, LX3, GW, FPS, tv). Assign -1 to -2 to the following consonant fragment or tail. Tokens with vowels do NOT trigger the negative pole, even when they are odd. Instead, rare-word or acronym pieces that contain vowels (JAK, RO, CAN, DE, sam, Son, PE) get +1 to +2. Ordinary dictionary words get 0.

expl.label: Slot-opening predicates (+) vs. stock-phrase completions (−); diffuse, context-driven
expl.positive_pole: Tokens that open a slot where new, specific descriptive content is about to follow. Typical cases: a subject plus auxiliary or verb that introduces a description or attribute ("the words| stay", "These items| have| never", "floors| are|/can", "Russell is described| as", "police| will"). Also purpose or lead-in markers like "to write| a", "In addition| to", "onto which| we'll| hand|write", "codes| for", "being| of". Also list/spec scaffolding in descriptive or listing text: "what you'll| learn|:", "opportunity to:↵|-", dashes or newlines starting the next amenity ("garage↵–"), commas between adjectives in hotel/property blurbs ("comfortable, clean, modern rooms"), and numeric fields in specs, timestamps or page numbers ("Slipcase 30 x 20", "T14:25:33", "Page 1679", "(0.004 inch)"). Common genres are property/product/hotel blurbs, announcements and expository definitions.
expl.negative_pole:
Tokens that complete a highly conventional collocation or formulaic sequence whose content is already essentially determined, mostly in instructional, legal, recipe, scientific or listing boilerplate. Examples:
- the middle or late item of a stock triad: "technical,| administrative| and physical" (−8); "refuse, edit,| or| remove" (−7); "Paraphrasing| and| Summarizing" (−8)
- recipe steps: "cream butter, sugar, and vanilla… Add| eggs" (−7)
- software boilerplate: "Click OK to close the dialog| box" (−7)
- times: "8:15 p|.m" (−7)
- dimension and formula notation: "12.5cm x| 300cm", "(z)(15)" (−8)
- dates: "created in| 2004" (−7)
- set phrases: "portrayed in| meditation", "boxes for| the connoisseur"
- an anaphoric pronoun continuing an expected scientific narrative: "capillaries| it| is collected" (−10)
expl.rubric:
Background is about 0 on most tokens; about 7% of tokens reach |1|, and scattered ±1 values are common almost everywhere.

Positive values:
- +1 to +2: function words and commas inside descriptive or spec text.
- +3 to +6: the auxiliary/verb, preposition or colon that launches a description, specification or list item.
- +5 to +8: rare cases where a subject noun or verb strongly sets up an upcoming specification ("the words" +8, "write a" +8, "cover versions" +6, "you'll learn" +6).
- Digits in timestamps or dimensions can reach +3 to +6.

Negative values:
- −1 to −3: diffuse scatter.
- −4 to −10: the token that completes a formulaic sequence, such as a stock triad item, a unit or notation continuation ("p.m", "x", "cm", "box"), or a recipe or UI step verb/noun.

Other notes:
- Numbers can go either way: numeric fields being set up lean positive, while completing a formula or unit leans negative.
- Plain narrative prose stays near 0.
- When unsure, predict 0 to ±1.

expl.label: Digits in numbers: label-value starts (+) vs. 'or/($/Save' equivalents (−)
expl.positive_pole: The first digits (and leading space) of a number that is the primary value directly after a label or operator: 'Frac part = (0.62', 'added: 2012', 'apartments: 112', 'Sum of prime factors: 1215', 'main city beach: 600m', '3 - 02:37', '1872 - 1944'. Also fires on joining operators between quantities, such as '+' in '3.99 + free shipping', 'x' multipliers, '5+', and 'for every'. The activation sits on the space or digit just after ':', '=', '-', or '+'. Weak positive (~+1) appears on scattered tokens in names, addresses and titles.
expl.negative_pole: Digits (and the '$', '£', '(+' or ',' tokens) of a secondary, alternative, restated or derived quantity that follows a first figure. Typical triggers: 'or $22,000' (conversion/alternative price), 'Save £7.50', 'Save 20% ($0.50', '(+15/Level', '(24 y, 1 m, 18 d', 'yards or 3281', a parenthetical local time '(7:33 a', a currency conversion after '£43,000; $85', 'about 160', 'an average of one every 8', 'maximum +25'. The strongest values land on the first digit or currency symbol right after 'or', 'Save', '($' or '(', and fade over the following digits.
expl.rubric: Background is 0 for nearly all tokens, including prose and most numbers in running text. Negative pole: the first digit or currency token of an equivalent/alternative/savings/parenthetical-conversion amount scores -5 to -10 (e.g. 'or $2|-10 2,000', 'Save £|-8 7|-3 .|-4 5|-6'). Subsequent digits in that number score -1 to -4. Weaker cases ('about 160', 'average of', '(+15') score -3 to -6. Ordinary digits inside numbers in price/stat lists score about -1. Positive pole: a number starting right after a label colon, '=', or a dash range/time scores +2 to +5 on the first digit or the preceding space, then +1 to +3 on the following digits. Operators '+' and 'x' between quantities score +2 to +4. Weak +1 appears on random tokens in addresses, song titles and credits. Not firing: numbers inside plain narrative sentences (near 0 or -1) and non-numeric text.

expl.label: Slot for a new contrasting value in repeated parallel structures (+); copied phrases and examples (−)
expl.positive_pole: The neuron fires when text sets up a parallel or repeated template (lists, contrasts, A-vs-B sentences, repeated rows) and reaches the slot where a new, differing value is about to appear. The activation sits on the token just before that value, or on the value itself. Examples: 'The Horans have four daughters, and the Butzens have **two** sons' (fires on 'two'); 'array of seven arrays, each of them consisting **of 50**'; 'such as the United States, Canada**,** **or** Mexico'; 'Base 5 and **Base 12**'; 'for sale in Salt Lake City, for rent **in** Salt Lake City'; 'from Black Panther **to** Iron Man **to** Scarlet Witch'; 'Nissan, Honda**,** Acura'; a stock row 'Grade 3: £3.99 - **0** in stock'; 'the **'**70s'; 'with low mileage, others prefer ones with **the** lowest price'; dates in a list like '8/16/17, 9**/**6'. The neuron is anticipating the varying element of the second or later instance of the pattern. The first instance gets little activation.
expl.negative_pole: Tokens inside an illustrative example or quoted instance, or a near-verbatim reuse of an earlier phrase where content is being copied rather than varied. Examples: dictionary example sentences after 'definition 2:' ('- They **are** about **the** office', about −7); 'Example: to offer **someone a**' (about −6); 'Resolutions are "I want to **get** an agent"' (about −5); requirement specs ('user must be **able** to', about −5); 'For **example**, a job...' (about −4); a repeated phrase 'With notably rare exceptions**,**' (about −5); a repeated menu path 'User's menu -> settings -> **messages**' (about −4); 'It's **a** Girl' after 'It's a Boy' (about −3); 'Windows **7**' after 'Windows Vista was version 6.0' (about −3); a reformatted time 'tod at **7:**00' (about −7).
expl.rubric: Background is 0. Broad diffuse ±1 values are scattered across ordinary prose; about 2.6% of tokens reach |value|≥1, and values ≥3 are very rare. Score +4 to +10 for the token at or just before the differing value in a second or later parallel item. The strongest cases have a clear prior template that is now being refilled with a new number, name or quantity: numbers, list connectors ('or', 'and', ',', 'to', 'in'), or the noun or head word opening the new item. Score +1 to +3 for weaker list commas, or the first hint of a repeated frame. Score −3 to −7 for tokens inside example sentences, quoted illustrations, or verbatim or reformatted repetitions of an earlier phrase, especially function words and verbs in the copied span. Score 0 for first mentions and ordinary non-parallel text.

expl.label: Tokens inside formal reference identifiers: citation numbers, paths, category strings
expl.positive_pole: Tokens in the middle of a formal identifier or reference string, especially after a designator that tells the reader a specific code or path is coming. The identifier tokens themselves fire, not the designator. Examples: journal volume and page numbers (Phys. Rev. B 71553), patent numbers (U.S. patent 7,266,205), statute and regulation numbers (MINN. STAT. 176.2; 50 CFR 40; Title 17; Stats. 2001), SIC codes, FreeBSD/CVS paths (usr/ports/X11, ports/security, pgsql-server/src/backend), category paths (category "Antiques\Furniture"; Subjects: | R Medicine > R), and UI navigation steps (go to the File menu; click on; choose). Activation is strongest a few tokens into a numeric or path sequence. The peak is the 3rd–5th digit of a citation number (~+10).
expl.negative_pole: Very weak, at most about -1. It shows up on tokens just before a small count or value in boilerplate: 'All times are GMT -4', 'The following 33 pages', 'Page 1 of 2', and on colons in metadata lines such as 'Date posted:', 'Difficulty:' and 'located in this country:'.
expl.rubric:
Background is 0 for almost all tokens, including ordinary prose, ordinary numbers, dates and prices. Assign values as follows:
- Citation, patent or volume-page digit strings: +2 to +10, peaking mid-sequence. Typical values are +4 to +7, with the max ~+10 on the 3rd–5th digit of a journal citation. Commas inside the number get about +4.
- Software path segments ('ports', '/backend', '1' in X11): +1 to +4. The repository name after a path separator gets ~+4.
- The opening quote after 'in the category' gets ~+2 to +3; the next path pieces get ~+1.
- Taxonomy separators ('|', '>') in metadata fields: +2 to +4.
- Legal code numbers: +1 to +2.
- UI instruction verbs and prepositions ('go to', 'click on', 'choose'): +1 to +2.
- Ticker or code openings like '(LOV' and numeric fields after 'SIC code:': ~+1 to +2.
- Negatives (only about -1): the space or dash before a small count in forum or wiki boilerplate ('GMT -4', 'following 33', 'Page 1 of 2') and colons in metadata such as 'Date posted:'.
Does not fire on normal numbers in prose, on years or dates in narrative, or on generic text.

expl.label: Action verb/gerund heading the task someone undertakes (how to X, before entering)
expl.positive_pole: Fires on the verb (often gerund or bare infinitive) naming an action or undertaking that a person or agent performs, in contexts that frame it as a task, process, or endeavor. Typical frames: 'how to implement', 'what it was like to live in', 'before entering this space', 'how to go about troubleshooting', 'Those using these images', 'interested in applying for', 'required for the auditor to deliver', 'what goes into making', 'carrying out research', 'the costs of renting', 'Passing this test', 'People who experience'. Clause- or sentence-initial gerunds/infinitives also fire ('Finding the best website', 'To create a new', 'Doing'). The peak sits on the main action verb. The framing words leading up to it (how/to/before/for/into/of) ramp up at +1 to +5. Particles or prepositions completing the phrasal verb can carry the peak too ('get your hands on' +9 on 'on', 'go about' +8, 'carrying out' +8). Weaker spillover follows on the object (this/one/a +1 to +4).
expl.negative_pole: Weak, max about -4.
